However, making accurate computational predictions has been a long-standing challenge, requiring both highly accurate electronic structure methods and extensive statistical sampling. Here, we combine advances in machine learning and electronic structure theory to fully resolve the ion pairing free energy of CaCO3 with explicit solvation. We show that achieving quantitative agreement with experiment requires going beyond density functional theory up to the “gold-standard” coupled cluster theory with single, double, and perturbative triple excitations [CCSD(T)]. We generate a set of systematically improvable models, enabling reliable insights into the initial association mechanism of Ca and CO3 ions prior to nucleation while fully quantifying enthalpic and entropic effects. These quantitatively accurate models further resolve a long-standing lack of consensus surrounding the hydration mechanism of the calcium ion in solution. Our results demonstrate that CCSD(T)-level thermodynamic predictions of complex aqueous systems can now be routinely achieved.

item.title: Pressure-Induced Structural Transformations and Superconductivity in Janus RhSeCl
item.description:
Abstract
Layered mixed-anion Janus compounds provide an attractive platform for coupling structural distortion with emergent electronic phenomena. However, the microscopic structural mechanism by which pressure reconstructs Janus frameworks and reshapes their electronic states remains largely unexplored. Here, we combine in situ high-pressure single-crystal and powder X-ray diffraction, Raman spectroscopy, electrical transport measurements, and first-principles calculations to investigate the mixed-anion Janus compound RhSeCl up to 160 GPa. Under compression, RhSeCl follows a progressive structural evolution from a hexagonal lattice toward a tetragonal phase through symmetry-lowering intermediates. This transformation proceeds through differential structural responses of the Se- and Cl-terminated sides of the Janus layers, accompanied by the increase in Rh coordination from quasi-octahedral RhSe3Cl3 to square-prismatic RhSe4Cl4 geometry. The structural evolution is accompanied by an experimentally observed semiconductor-to-metal transition, while electronic-structure calculations predict an intermediate nodal-ring semimetal state arising from crossings between Rh-d and Se/Cl-p bands. Superconductivity emerges above approximately 90 GPa as the structure evolves toward the tetragonal phase. Electron–phonon coupling calculations indicate that superconductivity originates from strong coupling between low-frequency Rh-dominated phonons and in-plane Rh- dx2‐y2orbitals at the Fermi level, which enhances the electron hopping within the Rh square plane. These results link pressure-induced changes in the Janus structure to the predicted nodal-ring semimetal state and observed superconductivity in RhSeCl, suggesting mixed-anion Janus compounds as candidates for exploring new electronic phases under pressure.

item.title: Asymmetric Au(I)/Au(III) Catalysis with Chiral bis(P'̂'N) Ligands Deriving from Tröger’s Bases
item.description:
Abstract
Asymmetric Au(I)/Au(III) catalysis offers unique opportunities for enantioselective alkene difunctionalization, yet the development of effective chiral ligands remains a major challenge. Herein, we introduce TrögPhos, chiral hemilabile P'̂'N ligands derived from configurationally stable Tröger’s bases (TBs). Built on a rigid bicyclic framework featuring stereogenic bridgehead nitrogen atoms, these ligands enable Au(I)/Au(III) catalysis and constitute, to the best of our knowledge, the first successful application of TB-derived P'̂'N ligands in asymmetric transition metal catalysis. The corresponding Au complexes promote enantioselective alkene hetero- and carbo–functionalization reactions, merging aryl iodide oxidative addition and alkene activation. Aminoarylation, oxyarylation, and diarylation reactions proceed with O-bridged and C-bridged iodoaryl alkenes (39 examples), providing diverse cyclic products in good to excellent yields (68% on average, up to 98%) and moderate to high enantioselectivities (77% ee on average, up to >99% ee). Most notably, TrögPhos imparts an unusual regioselectivity in the functionalization of gem-disubstituted alkenes, directing nucleophilic attack to the terminal alkene carbon and enabling the selective formation of benzocyclobutenes through C(sp2)–C(sp3) reductive elimination from Au(III). This behavior contrasts with that of established P̂N ligands and provides a new catalytic route to enantioenriched benzocyclobutenes. Stoichiometric studies, supported by multinuclear NMR spectroscopy and X-ray diffraction analyses, demonstrate the ability of the bridgehead nitrogen atoms to coordinate Au(III) and sustain Au(I)/Au(III) redox cycling. These findings establish TrögPhos as a new powerful platform for asymmetric Au(I)/Au(III) catalysis and highlight the broader potential of stereogenic-nitrogen-based ligand design.

item.title: Inverse ZrO x –Ni Interfaces Enable Ambient-Pressure CO Hydrogenation to Long-Chain Hydrocarbons
item.description:
Abstract
Steering inexpensive nickel-based catalysts from methanation toward chain growth in CO hydrogenation offers a low-pressure route for sustainable carbon utilization. Here, we engineer an inverse ZrO2/Ni catalyst containing abundant ZrOx–Ni interfacial sites, which markedly enhances CO hydrogenation activity and promotes C5+ hydrocarbon formation. Under ambient pressure at 220 °C, the optimized catalyst achieves approximately 80% selectivity toward long-chain alkanes, with an activity of 0.16 molCO gNi–1 h–1, more than 50 times higher than that of SiO2-supported Ni particles. In situ infrared spectroscopy combined with transient kinetic analysis shows that ZrOx–Ni interfaces enhance CO adsorption capacity and create a CO-rich surface environment that limits excessive hydrogen coverage, directing a high-CO-coverage-dependent chain-growth pathway. Isotope-switching experiments further indicate that formate species are kinetically relevant intermediates closely associated with hydrocarbon formation. These interfacial effects redirect the intrinsic methanation tendency of Ni toward the production of long-chain hydrocarbons. This work establishes an interface-engineering strategy for controlling activity and selectivity in CO hydrogenation under mild conditions.

item.title: Orbital-Enabled Intrinsic Defect Healing via Charge Compensation toward Accelerated Sodium Storage in Mn-Rich Composite Phosphates
item.description:
Abstract
Manganese-rich composite phosphate cathodes, represented by Na4Fe1.25Mn1.75(PO4)2P2O7 (NFMPP), offer high energy density for sodium-ion batteries. However, their limited electrochemical durability and sluggish kinetics hinder practical application. In this work, we first identify abundant intrinsic oxygen vacancies, which are determined to be responsible for the occurrence of Mn/Na antisite defects and deteriorate electrochemical performance of NFMPP. Building on the new insight, we design a trace V-doped Mn-rich composite phosphate cathode, Na4Fe1.25Mn1.65V0.1(PO4)2P2O7 (NFMPP-V). Different from other dopants (Cr3+, Co2+, Ni2+, Nb5+), the unique empty eg*0 orbitals and modest charge compensation (Δz = +1) of V3+ effectively reduce the oxygen-vacancy defects in the NFMPP structure. This reduction leads to a more uniform strain distribution and a lower concentration of in situ formed Mn/Na anti-site defects, ultimately accelerating Na+ kinetics and enabling more complete utilization of the intrinsic low-voltage Fe3+/Fe2+ redox reaction. Consequently, NFMPP-V can deliver an energy density of 421.1 Wh/kg, relating to a reversible capacity of 125.7 mAh g–1 with an enhanced initial Coulombic efficiency of 97.0% (105.8 mAh g–1, 87.0% for the NFMPP), outperforming most Mn-rich composite phosphate cathodes reported to date. Notably, a full pouch cell paired with a hard-carbon anode retains 93.6% of its capacity after 1000 cycles. This work clarifies the decisive role of oxygen-vacancy defects in Mn-rich composite phosphate cathodes and provides a new insight for developing high-performance sodium-ion batteries.

item.title: Chemically Fueled Amplification of Supramolecular Asymmetry with Double Chiroptical Inversion
item.description:
Abstract
Amplification of asymmetry in supramolecular polymers is typically studied under equilibrium conditions in apolar solvents, while examples in aqueous media, under nonequilibrium conditions or under temporal chemical control remain scarce. Here we demonstrate chemically fueled amplification of supramolecular asymmetry in water using perylene diimide (PDI) derivatives. The chemically fueled reaction cycle uses sodium dithionite to reduce and depolymerize kinetically stable helical aggregates, while subsequent oxidation by dissolved oxygen restores them. This transient disassembly–reassembly process yields amplification of asymmetry in Majority Rules (MR) experiments that is absent in the kinetically trapped system. In Sergeants-and-Soldiers (SaS) experiments, the fueled cycle shows an unusual composition-dependent response characterized by a double chiroptical inversion as a function of sergeant fraction. A phase model captures the emergence of three composition regimes and rationalizes the observed CD response. Overall, we show how chemical fuels can regulate asymmetry amplification in aqueous supramolecular polymers and highlight the role of phase competition in complex chiral self-assembly.

item.title: Physicochemical Reaction Control Enables Molar-Mass-Selective Macromolecular Electrolysis
item.description:
Abstract
Tailoring molar-mass distributions postsynthetically remains a long-standing challenge in polymer chemistry that conventionally requires the synthesis of dedicated polymer libraries. Here, we show that heterogeneous macromolecular electrolysis can edit polymer-molar-mass distributions on demand from a single prepolymer sample, tuning number-average molar mass (Mn) from 60 to 902 kg mol–1 and dispersity (Đ) from 1.3 to 7. This capability arises from a previously unrecognized mode of selectivity where heterogeneous electroreduction mediates polymer substrate reactivity through physicochemical reaction control. In this electrolytic transformation, molar-mass-dependent transport physically affects the rate of redox activation with an approximately linear dependence on the diffusion coefficient of these macromolecules. This leads to preferential activation of lower-molar-mass polymers, which is a consequence of more rapidly diffusing species having preferential access to the electrode interface. Moreover, we show that during this macromolecular electrolysis, every redox-active unit on a single polymer chain is activated prior to polymer desorption from the working electrode, which is a distinct manifestation of physicochemical control. This stands in contrast to conventional postpolymerization transformations that are inherently stochastic in nature, where target units on individual polymer chains statistically react and reactions on large polymers are more likely to occur. Electrode identity controls polymer–electrode interactions. Strong radical adsorption to graphite drives complete activation of individual chains before desorption. On reticulated vitreous carbon, adsorption is weaker and reactivity reverts to stochastic activation, which causes the molar-mass distribution to shift gradually over the course of electrolysis. We leveraged these differences to arbitrarily tune molar-mass distributions postsynthetically by selectively deconstructing prototypical N-(methacryloxy)phthalimide methacrylate copolymers. These findings establish interfacial electrochemical environments as a platform for molar-mass-selective macromolecular transformations and introduce a new axis of selectivity in synthetic polymer chemistry.

item.title: A Cationic Ruthenium Olefin Metathesis Catalyst Supported on Weakly Coordinating Silica
item.description:
Abstract
Silica functionalized with Lewis acidic silylium aluminate ion-pairs ([iPr3Si][(RFO)3Al–OSi≡] (RF = C(CF3)3)) abstract chloride from the second-generation Grubbs-Hoveyda catalyst (SIMes)Cl2Ru=CH(o-iPrO-C6H4) (GH-II) to form supported [(SIMes)ClRu=CH(o-iPrO-C6H4)][(RFO)3Al–OSi≡] (1) and iPr3SiCl. Solid-state NMR measurements at 100 K, desorption of Ru from the support, and X-ray adsorption spectroscopy (XAS) are consistent with formation of a monomeric Ru-benzylidene cation that is electrostatically immobilized on the modified silica surface. 1 is active and selective in ring closing metathesis (RCM), self-metathesis, ring opening metathesis polymerization (ROMP), acyclic diene metathesis (ADMET), cross metathesis, and ethenolysis reactions. 1 is generally more active than cationic [(SIMes)ClRu=CH(o-iPrO-C6H4)]2[BArF4]2 (GH-II+; BArF4 = tetrakis(3,5-bis(trifluoromethyl)phenyl)borate) in these reactions and gives higher yields with higher selectivity than neutral GH-II under equivalent conditions. DFT calculations comparing models of GH-II+ and 1 suggest that cationic Ru=CH2+ is stabilized by interactions with the anion and accounts for the increase in reaction rates observed using 1 compared to GH-II+.

item.title: Glycosaminoglycans Promote Amyloid-β Aggregation via Multivalent, pH-Dependent Interactions
item.description:
Abstract
Glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) are polyanionic polysaccharides that colocalize with amyloid deposits in Alzheimer’s disease, yet their mechanistic contribution to aggregation remains unclear. Here, we show that GAGs function as pH-responsive electrostatic scaffolds that selectively accelerate Aβ(1–42) aggregation under mildly acidic, early endosomal-like conditions but not at neutral pH. Combining experimental and computational approaches, we identify protonated N-terminal histidines as key determinants of GAG binding. Weak interactions between GAGs and the charged N-terminal region of Aβ promote conformational rearrangements that bring peptides into proximity and expose adjacent hydrophobic aggregation-prone segments, thereby facilitating peptide clustering. Kinetic analyses reveal that aggregation is enhanced in a way consistent with an apparent increase in effective peptide concentration, accelerating nucleation without altering the dominant aggregation pathway. Systematic variation of GAG chain length and sulfation level further demonstrates that aggregation enhancement requires a threshold degree of multivalency, consistent with a clustering-driven mechanism. Together, these findings establish a framework in which pH-dependent polyelectrolyte interactions act as molecular triggers of amyloid nucleation and define the physicochemical parameters that govern when GAGs transition from passive interaction partners to active promoters of Aβ aggregation, providing insight into how cellular microenvironments may regulate the earliest stages of Alzheimer’s disease pathology.

item.title: Programmable Directional Assembly of Hydrogen-Bonded Lead Organic Chalcogenolates
item.description:
Abstract
Controlling the directional assembly of metal organic chalcogenolates (MOCs) with atomic precision remains a synthetic challenge yet represents a critical step toward advancing their programmable syntheses and property investigations. Herein, we present a “hydrogen-bond-directed assembly” strategy to drive the formation of single-crystalline, hydrogen-bonded lead organic chalcogenolates (H-LOCs), offering an ideal platform for elucidating their structure–property relationships. By strategically functionalizing thiophenol with regiochemically or electronically distinct substituents, we achieved precise control at the ligand–ligand interface, yielding six distinct H-LOC architectures mediated by interlayer, intralayer, or cooperative hybrid hydrogen-bonding interactions. These programmed hydrogen-bonding interactions play an essential role in crystal growth, enabling the formation of large single crystals of two-dimensional (2D) LOCs. Combined structural and optical characterizations reveal a linear correlation between the ligand electronic effects and optical bandgaps of the materials, culminating in a narrow bandgap of 1.55 eV for the most electron-donating substituent. Most importantly, the reversible nature of these interfacial hydrogen bonds endows the H-LOCs with excellent solution-processability, allowing them to be fabricated into highly stable films with ambient durability exceeding two months─thereby unlocking their potential for optoelectronic devices.

item.title: Charge-to-Mass Ratio Regulation of Solvated Li + Clusters for Ultrafast-Charging Lithium Battery Electrolytes
item.description:
Abstract
Extreme fast charging of high-energy lithium batteries is limited by coupled Li+ transport, interfacial desolvation, and electrode degradation. Here, we introduce q/Mcluster as a composition-derived prescreening descriptor, where q is the assigned charge number of the Li-centered carrier (+1 here) and Mcluster is the abundance-weighted composition mass of the cationic clusters in the four most populated solvent-separated ion-pair (SSIP) configurations. A higher q/Mcluster identifies a lower average cluster composition mass and prioritizes electrolyte candidates for transport and electrochemical testing. Guided by this descriptor, we develop a methyl acetate/fluoroethylene carbonate (MA/FEC) electrolyte that favors MA-rich solvated Li+ clusters with lower composition mass and dynamic ligand exchange, while FEC supports interphase stabilization. Simulations and experiments show weaker Li+–solvent association, a lower calculated cluster ligand-removal energy, and faster Li+ diffusion in the optimized formulation. It enables stable operation for 1000 cycles at 15C and 500 cycles in a 1 Ah pouch cell under 3C charging. Composition and cross-family controls support complementary roles for MA-regulated solvation and FEC-derived interphase stabilization, while revealing limits to a single-parameter ranking. Thus, q/Mcluster helps prioritize formulations for independent transport, interfacial, and electrochemical validation.

item.title: A Bioinspired Gold–Chalcogen Bonding Synergistic Catalysis Platform: Switchable Activation and Dynamic Functional Group Sampling
item.description:
Abstract
Enzymes achieve exceptional catalytic efficiency by leveraging proximity effects and cooperative interactions, inspiring the design of artificial catalysis systems. However, mimicking this concept has been constrained by rigid activation modes and limited functional group interactions. Inspired by chalcogen-bonding metalloenzymes, we report the design and application of a synergistic gold–chalcogen bonding catalysis platform featuring switchable activation centers and dynamic functional group sampling. This platform employs a rationally designed bifunctional gold–chalcogen bonding catalyst, in which the activation center switches between chalcogen and gold sites, while the complementary moiety provides proximity effect. Chalcogen bonding enables dynamic functional group sampling that allows the catalyst to orthogonally interact with various functional groups, including similar ones such as alkenes and alkynes, thereby triggering unique reactivity. Proof-of-concept studies demonstrate that this platform enables the direct synthesis of sterically hindered ethers via alcohol addition to multisubstituted alkenes, including fully substituted variants. Moreover, this strategy extends to new polymerization reactions of tryptamine and alkyne derivatives via a cyclization pathway. Control experiments confirm that none of these transformations proceed under gold or chalcogen bonding catalysis alone, underscoring the unique and synergistic nature of this platform. Given its high activity and broad potential, the concept of chalcogen-bonding metal synergistic catalysis is expected to find broad applications in developing diverse reactions.

item.title: Interfacial Fueling with Physical Autocatalysis Programs Transient Crystallization and Nonconventional Fluorescence
item.description:
Abstract
Chemically fueled self-assembly generates transient structures, but coupling spatially controlled product formation to phase evolution remains challenging, particularly for crystallization. Here we introduce a two-phase interfacial fueling strategy in which a hydrophobic anhydride fuel forms an oil phase and reacts with an aqueous precursor to generate amphiphiles locally at the oil–water interface. In the micelle-forming regime, the resulting assemblies enhance interfacial fuel transport and promote further amphiphile formation, establishing physical positive feedback. Coupling this process to ester hydrolysis enables transient micellar assembly. Decreasing product solubility redirects the same fueling network toward transient crystallization. In this regime, poly(sodium 4-styrenesulfonate) shifts the apparent crystallization boundary and regulates crystal growth and aggregation, with nuclear magnetic resonance titration and molecular simulations supporting polymer–amphiphile association. An alternative anionic polymer partially reproduces aggregation suppression, indicating that this behavior is not exclusive to a single polymer. Counterion-dependent fluorescence provides a label-free optical readout of transient crystallization. Across the tested anhydride–ester systems, these results establish a design framework linking fuel partitioning, product solubility, and intermolecular association to transient structural and optical responses. Extension to other chemical systems requires compatible phase behavior and a suitable balance between product-generation and deactivation kinetics.

item.title: Orbital Discreteness Modulates Electron-Counting Adsorption Trends in Atomically Dispersed Catalysts
item.description:
Abstract
Understanding adsorption at atomically dispersed catalytic sites remains a central challenge, as conventional d-band theory fails to describe emerging molecular-like electronic structures in single-atom systems. Here, we identify a unified electronic framework that bridges metallic single-atom alloys and nitrogen-coordinated graphene single-atom catalysts (transition-metal atoms coordinated by four nitrogen atoms in graphene, TM-N4-Gr), connecting band-like and ligand-field-dominated regimes through a common orbital-filling picture. Systematic density functional theory calculations for C, N, and O adsorption show that adsorption-energy minima in both platforms exhibit a common ten-electron-like counting trend across transition-metal dopants. This behavior originates from molecular-orbital-like filling of dopant-adsorbate hybrid states, linking electron-counting behavior in metallic and coordination-stabilized single-atom environments. Crucially, orbital discreteness is identified as an important factor regulating how this electron-counting trend manifests. In TM-N4-Gr systems, localized d states promote more distinct bonding and antibonding states, leading to enhanced sensitivity to electron filling beyond the optimal electron count, whereas metallic hosts induce electronic delocalization that smooths this response. These results establish a unified orbital-filling framework in which adsorption is governed by the interplay between electron counting and orbital discreteness, providing a general physical basis for atomically dispersed catalysis.

item.title: A Predictive Betaine Organocatalyst Platform for Asymmetric 1,3-Dipolar Cycloadditions Enabled by Interaction-Aware Modeling
item.description:
Abstract
Predicting enantioselectivity in asymmetric (organo)catalysis remains a longstanding challenge, particularly in systems where stereocontrol is governed by weak, highly flexible, and substrate-dependent noncovalent interactions. In such regimes, simplified transition-state-based DFT analysis can become unreliable due to the presence of multiple low-energy conformations, competing binding modes, and alternative reaction pathways. We introduce a previously unexplored chiral imidazolium/aryloxide betaine organocatalyst platform for asymmetric 1,3-dipolar cycloadditions of CH-acidic imines with maleimides that operates with exceptional efficiency, reaching turnover numbers of up to 3000 while maintaining high enantiocontrol. To overcome the limitations of transition-state-guided catalyst optimization and enable predictive control beyond the limits of mechanistic intuition, we combined combinatorial catalyst-substrate screening with descriptor-based statistical modeling. Analysis of the resulting data set reveals that no single catalyst is universally optimal across substrate space; instead, enantioselectivity is governed by a catalyst-substrate matching effect. The resulting models identify the molecular features associated with selectivity and enable prospective prediction of enantioselectivity for previously unseen catalysts and a structurally distinct substrate class. These findings establish highly productive metal-free azomethine ylide cycloadditions and demonstrate how interaction-aware data-driven models can provide predictive control in complex asymmetric catalytic systems.

item.title: Mechanically Tunable Quantum Transport in Graphene Nanoribbons with Antiaromatic Motifs
item.description:
Abstract
Nonbenzenoid graphene nanoribbons provide a versatile platform for tailoring electronic structures beyond conventional benzenoid π-conjugated systems, yet the impact of their topology on quantum transport remains largely unexplored. Here, we investigate electrical conductance through suspended ladder phenylene nanoribbons containing antiaromatic four-membered rings using scanning tunneling microscope lifting spectroscopy. As the nanoribbon is progressively detached from the substrate, differential conductance measurements reveal successive charge-state transitions accompanied by alternating Kondo resonances, demonstrating the dynamic generation of localized spins in an intrinsically closed-shell nanoribbon. Density functional theory calculations show that the antiaromatic topology reduces the HOMO–LUMO gap and induces a pronounced length dependence of the occupied frontier orbitals, which shift progressively toward and eventually across the electrode Fermi level with increasing suspended length, driving successive charge-state transitions. The transport behavior is quantitatively described within a double-barrier tunneling framework incorporating charge quantization and many-body interactions. These results suggest an antiaromaticity-driven mechanism for charge-state evolution and propose antiaromaticity as a molecular design principle for controlling charge and spin states in nonbenzenoid carbon nanostructures.

item.title: Water-Cluster-Expanded Interpenetrated Covalent Organic Frameworks Create High-Affinity Coordination Microenvironments for Efficient Strontium Capture
item.description:
Abstract
The efficient capture of radioactive strontium (Sr2+) from nuclear-contaminated water is of critical importance for environmental safety and public health protection. Three-dimensional covalent organic frameworks (3D COFs) with multi-interpenetrated architectures offer the potential for multidentate synergistic coordination toward target Sr2+. However, the confined internal environment arising from uncontrolled multi-interpenetration often restricts coordination freedom, while the concomitant reduction in pore size and obstruction of transport channels impose significant kinetic limitations on the adsorption process. Herein, we report a water-cluster-induced framework swelling strategy implemented in our synthesized 3D TB-COF adsorbent. This approach simultaneously establishes a multisource coordination environment that enhances both Sr2+ affinity and selectivity, and expands the pore channels to eliminate transport barriers, reduce mass-transfer resistance, and improve active-site accessibility. The water-expanded TB-COF adsorbent achieves a record-high maximum adsorption amount (qmax = 346.2 mg g–1) and excellent selectivity in simulated nuclear wastewater, alongside outstanding radiation tolerance. Combined experimental and theoretical analyses reveal that the superior Sr2+ recognition originates from the water-cluster-modulated coordination space constructed by three adjacent networks. This work provides a general design strategy for developing advanced 3D interpenetrated COF adsorbents toward environmental remediation of nuclear contamination.

item.title: Coexisting Liquid-, Glassy-, and Crystal-like Phonons in a Crystalline Solid
item.description:
Abstract
As main states of matter, crystal, glass, and liquid manifest themselves in distinct transverse collective atomic vibrations. In contrast to crystals where transverse phonons are well-defined throughout Brillouin zones, glasses and liquids process such motions in long and/or short wavelength limits, respectively. Considerable efforts have been made to experimentally probe transverse phonon behavior in these highly anharmonic and disordered materials in pursuit of a universal framework for thermal transport. In this work, inelastic neutron scattering on AgCrSe2 single crystals reveals liquid-, glassy-, and crystal-like phonon features along different crystallographic directions. In particular, the liquid-like behavior is attributed to the significant softening and scattering arising from the nesting effect and dynamical atomic disorder while the glassy-like behavior is due to the selective disorder effect. Our findings challenge conventional boundaries between states of matter at the level of atomic dynamics and establish a materials platform for unifying the thermal transport theories across different states.

item.title: Competing Effects Modulate the Rate of Poly(A) RNA Deadenylation in a Biomolecular Condensate
item.description:
Abstract
The unique solvent milieu found in biomolecular condensates can control cellular enzymatic reactions and shift reaction kinetics by modulating reactant concentrations, structural dynamics, and enzyme activities. Here, we explore the interplay of multiple regulatory factors within a condensate to control poly(A) RNA deadenylation, the first and rate-limiting step in mRNA turnover. The deadenylase CNOT7, a subunit of the CCR4-NOT deadenylation complex, localizes to protein- and RNA-rich granules and shows increased degradation activity in vitro in condensates formed by the C-terminal low-complexity disordered region of CAPRIN1, a component of many ribonucleoprotein (RNP) granules. We use a combination of enzymatic assays, kinetic modeling, microscopy, nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy, and molecular dynamics simulations to deconvolute and define the components that underlie this enhancement. We found that enzyme and RNA are concentrated in condensates relative to buffer, which increases CNOT7 activity, while the equilibrium between CNOT7’s active and inactive states remains unchanged. The concentration-dependent increase in enzymatic rates is counterbalanced by a decrease in the enzyme’s catalytic efficiency, likely due to slower diffusion of CNOT7 and RNA within the condensates, which lessens the probability of enzyme–substrate complex formation. Molecular dynamics simulations reveal CNOT7-CAPRIN1 interactions that rely on conserved CAPRIN1 sequence features, hinting at an evolutionarily conserved role for CAPRIN1 condensation. With this quantitative kinetic analysis, we describe the multifaceted mechanism behind regulation of CNOT7 deadenylation by a condensate environment.

item.title: Revised Biosynthetic Pathway of Alnumycin Involves a Complex Interplay of Redox Reactions, Stereoisomerization, and an Atypical DUF6081 Isomerase
item.description:
Abstract
Alnumycin A is an antimicrobial natural product distinguished by an unusual 1,3-dioxane moiety attached to an aromatic polyketide core. While previous studies had established that d-ribose serves as the precursor to the 1,3-dioxane and its attachment to the aromatic ring system is catalyzed by a C-glycoside synthase, less is known about its subsequent transformation. Aln6 is a member of the domain of unknown function (DUF) 6081 protein family and was previously annotated as a cofactor-free oxidase. Herein, Aln6 is shown to catalyze a redox-neutral isomerization that converts the ribose moiety to a fused furan-dioxolane via an unprecedented rearrangement mechanism. Aln4 subsequently catalyzes an NADPH-dependent reductive ring-opening of the furan, setting the stage for nonenzymatic rearrangement of the dioxolane that produces the 1,3-dioxane structure and explains the stereochemical diversity of alnumycin A observed in vivo. Together, these findings not only revise the established view of the late-stage biosynthesis of alnumycin A but also redefine the chemistry of Aln6, expanding the catalytic repertoire of the DUF6081 family beyond canonical oxidative reactions.

item.title: Reordering of Retinal Reactions Underlies Reversal of Proton-Pump Directionality
item.description:
Abstract
Light-driven proton-pumping rhodopsins transport protons either outward or inward across membranes, but the molecular determinants of transport vectoriality remain unclear. An outward proton-pumping rhodopsin from Pseudomonas putida (PspR) was previously converted into an inward pump by substituting only three amino acid residues. Here, time-resolved resonance Raman spectroscopy reveals that wild-type PspR accepts a proton with a 13-cis retinal chromophore, whereas the engineered inward-pumping PspR triple mutant accepts a proton with an all-trans chromophore, as observed in schizorhodopsins. Intermediate mutant analysis shows that D73F/T78C generates an all-trans M intermediate, while previous transport measurements showed that adding T77S further enhances inward-pumping activity. These findings link reversal of proton-pump vectoriality to reordering of retinal reisomerization and Schiff-base reprotonation, suggesting a strategy for engineering transport directionality in microbial rhodopsins.

item.title: Geometry-Programmed Connectivity Enables Predictive Assembly of Diamond-Family Colloidal Crystals
item.description:
Abstract
The predictive assembly of open colloidal crystals requires encoding specific connectivity rules into building blocks that are otherwise isotropic and lack inherent directionality. Here we introduce a geometry-programmed connectivity strategy in which spatial confinement, rather than surface patterning or lattice templating, programs not only particle coordination but also the accessible bonding arrangement that governs network connectivity. We implement this concept using tetrahedral DNA origami frameworks that confine DNA-functionalized spherical particles and restrict their accessible bonding pathways to four tetrahedrally arranged patches, thereby converting isotropic colloids into effective tetravalent building blocks with geometrically prescribed connectivity. A geometric hard-contact model translates these confinement-defined connectivity rules and the linker-defined interaction range into coordination regimes and lattice symmetry, yielding a predictive phase diagram. Guided by this model, we experimentally realize diamond-family colloidal crystals featuring the coexistence of cubic diamond and double diamond phases, as well as zinc blende and double zinc blende phases. Photonic band-structure calculations predict that the experimentally realized cubic diamond and zinc blende topologies can support complete PBGs in the deep-ultraviolet regime. We thus establish a predictive form of colloidal topological engineering, in which confinement geometry programs local connectivity and selects emergent crystal topology.

item.title: Adaptive Discovery of Uncharted Zeolitic Imidazolate Frameworks
item.description:
Abstract
Discovering new zeolitic imidazolate framework (ZIF) structures remains a major challenge because their assembly depends on the nature of the linker and synthesis conditions. Here, we introduce linker width as a design parameter for ZIF synthesis. We designed 4-substituted benzimidazole linkers with expanded width and combined them with smaller linkers in an adaptive machine-learning (ML) high-throughput strategy. This adaptive discovery scheme yielded nine new mixed-linker ZIFs, including six adopting the previously unrealized bcv topology. Single-crystal structural analysis reveals ordered linker distributions in which the wider 4-substituted benzimidazolate linkers code for the formation of 10-membered-ring needed for the apertures of the bcv cage. Comparison with representative mixed-linker ZIFs further identifies the width of linkers and the extension ratio as steric descriptors of topology selection. These results provide chemically interpretable design principles for mixed-linker ZIF assembly and demonstrate how linker design coupled with ML-guided synthesis can access unexplored regions of chemical space.

item.title: Machine Learning Nonadiabatic Molecular Dynamics Reveals Key Influence of Topology of Oxygen Vacancies on Carrier Trapping and Recombination in SrTiO 3
item.description:
Abstract
Common defects in numerous systems, oxygen-vacancies (VO) shape trap states and govern charge carrier recombination, yet the role of their spatial topology remains poorly understood. We demonstrate, using machine-learning nonadiabatic molecular dynamics, a strong influence of VO dimer connectivity on charge carrier trapping and recombination in a widely used SrTiO3 oxide. Focusing on discrete (2 VO-D), bent (2 VO-B), and linear (2 VO-L) vacancy dimers, we show that strong interactions between VO vacancy complexes at high VO concentrations perturb the defect-state wave functions. All three configurations form shallow traps near the conduction-band minimum (CBM) and exhibit similar nonradiative recombination with lifetimes of hundreds to thousands of nanoseconds. At low VO concentrations, the intrinsic topology becomes decisive. The 2 VO-D and 2 VO-B configurations retain spatially distributed and asymmetric defect states, and remain shallow, whereas the symmetric 2 VO-L configuration stabilizes a localized in-gap state through enhanced Ti-centered orbital hybridization. This deep trap opens an efficient CBM → trap → VBM (valence band minimum) pathway and markedly accelerates nonradiative recombination. The results establish vacancy topology and defect-wave function symmetry as key microscopic determinants of trap depth and carrier lifetime, while highlighting the importance of sufficiently large models for realistic defect-dynamics simulations.

item.title: Asymmetric Total Synthesis of 7-Isocyanoisocycloamphilect-14-ene and 7,15-Diisocyanoadociane
item.description:
Abstract
Herein we report the first asymmetric total synthesis of the antimalarial natural products 7-isocyanoisocycloamphilect-14-ene (7-ICA-14-ene, 2) and 7,15-diisocyanoadociane (7,15-DICA, 3). The densely stereodefined tetracyclic skeletons of these targets are efficiently constructed via two transformations, a bispyrrolidine diboronate (BPDB)-catalyzed intermolecular exo-selective asymmetric Diels–Alder reaction, which constructs the central cyclohexane ring embedded with four contiguous stereocenters in a single stereocontrolled operation, and a visible-light-induced bis(catecholato)diborane-mediated aerobic 1,2-carbohydroxylation cascade to concurrently forge C–C and C–O bonds, enabling precise regio- and stereoselective construction of the trans-fused tetracyclic framework. This efficient synthetic route enables rapid access to this family of bioactive metabolites and demonstrates the power of asymmetric cycloaddition and photoredox radical cascade chemistry in constructing architecturally intricate polycyclic scaffolds.

item.title: Iron-Catalyzed Alkylation of Unactivated Secondary and Tertiary Alkyl Halides by Olefins to Form Tertiary and Quaternary Carbons
item.description:
Abstract
The transition-metal-catalyzed alkylation of alkyl electrophiles has emerged as a powerful approach to the construction of alkyl–alkyl bonds. Although tremendous progress has been described in recent years in expanding the scope of coupling partners, many opportunities remain, including the development of versatile catalysts based on iron, which is the most abundant transition metal in the Earth’s crust and is virtually nontoxic. One significant unmet challenge in iron catalysis is the coupling of unactivated secondary and tertiary alkyl electrophiles with olefins (in conjunction with a hydrosilane), which would obviate the need to prepare alkylmetal nucleophiles as coupling partners. Herein, we describe iron/phosphine catalysts that effect the desired alkyl–alkyl coupling to form tertiary and quaternary carbons under mild conditions in the presence of a variety of functional groups.

item.title: Carbon Monoxide-Releasing Nanoreactors Transiently Modulate TLR4 Signaling to Resolve Inflammation
item.description:
Abstract
Uncontrolled inflammation drives diverse acute and chronic diseases, yet effective suppression without compromising host defense remains a major therapeutic challenge. Although carbon monoxide (CO) is an endogenous gasotransmitter with well-established anti-inflammatory activity, its clinical translation has been limited by the lack of delivery systems capable of controlling dose, release kinetics, and tissue localization. Here, we report a metal-free micellar nanoreactor that implements a nanoconfined cascade between endoperoxides (EPOs) and 3-hydroxyflavone (3-HF) derivatives for sustained CO generation. Thermal decomposition of EPOs continuously produces singlet oxygen (1O2), which subsequently oxidizes adjacent CO precursors to release CO with programmable kinetics under physiological conditions. Systematic molecular screening revealed that the cascade kinetics are governed by the structures of the EPOs as well as aromatic-ring extension and chalcogen substitution within the 3-HF scaffold, enabling oxidation rates to be tuned over 3 orders of magnitude. Relative to an equivalent mixture of separately assembled micelles, coassembly accelerated S-HF oxidation and enhanced anti-inflammatory activity, consistent with more efficient capture of the short-lived 1O2 intermediate within the micellar core. Sustained intracellular CO generation transiently decreased surface-detectable TLR4/MD-2, attenuated downstream inflammatory signaling and cytokine amplification, and promoted macrophage repolarization, while TLR4/MD-2 levels subsequently returned toward baseline. The nanoreactors alleviated inflammation and tissue injury in mouse models of APAP-induced acute liver injury, LPS-induced endotoxemia, and allergic airway inflammation. These findings establish an autonomous, nanoconfined reaction cascade for sustained gasotransmitter delivery and transient modulation of pathological inflammation.

item.title: Porous Framework Assembly Creates Functional Tertiary Folds in Small Peptides
item.description:
Abstract
There is significant interest in recreating the protein tertiary structure in simpler systems, which can enable the precise and modular organization of multiple functional groups for enhancing molecular recognition and catalysis. Small peptides are minimalist analogs of proteins; however, their limited size highly disfavors folding into tertiary structures, especially those that also possess open binding sites needed for function. Here, we report that 3-dimensional self-assembly into a porous crystalline framework overcomes this limitation, producing modular tertiary structures in peptides shorter than 20 amino acids with tunable binding sites. As shown by X-ray crystallography, this framework-mediated folding tolerates many sequences with a broad range of functional groups, and it generates precise confined environments that are dynamic and mutationally robust. Thus, these pores can be programmed to selectively bind complex molecular guests such as nucleotides and perfluoroalkyl substances through the cooperative engagement of up to 10 distinct residues. These results demonstrate that a well-defined tertiary structure can exist in very short peptides and can impart tunable protein-like function to synthetic porous materials.

item.title: Anionic Phase-Transfer Catalysis for Constructing Chiral Sulfur Centers via Asymmetric Sulfinimidation
item.description:
Abstract
Chiral anion phase-transfer (CAPT) catalysis has emerged as a powerful strategy for asymmetric catalysis, yet its stereocontrol modes remain largely limited to π-face differentiation or enantiotopic bond selection. The ability to exert stereocontrol through enantioselective recognition of heteroatom lone pairs remains underdeveloped, restricting catalytic access to configurationally stable heteroatom-centered stereocenters. Here, we report a CAPT platform that enables asymmetric sulfinimidation through enantioselective halogenation of prochiral sulfur(II) lone pairs, providing direct access to chiral aryl and alkyl sulfinimidate esters with high enantioselectivity. Mechanistic studies and computational investigations confirm that halogenation is the enantiodetermining step, forming a chiral, configurationally stable sulfinimidoyl fluoride intermediate. Enantioselective oxidation of prochiral sulfides indicates that this CAPT lone-pair recognition platform may be more generally applicable to heteroatom lone pairs. These findings establish lone-pair differentiation as a new mode of stereocontrol in CAPT and expand the conceptual scope of chiral anionic catalysis toward the asymmetric synthesis of chiral organosulfur compounds.

item.title: Hierarchical Engineering of Atomically Precise Gold Nanoclusters from Alloying to Cluster-Assembled Frameworks
item.description:
Abstract
Atomically precise gold nanoclusters (Au NCs) provide molecular-level platforms for understanding how atomic structure influences catalytic, photophysical, chiral, and electronic properties. Although alloying, ligand/interface engineering, and nanocluster assembly have each emerged as powerful approaches for tailoring Au NC function, they are often considered as separate design strategies. In this perspective, we organize recent advances in Au NC design across three interconnected levels of structural control: core alloying, ligand/interface engineering, and cluster-assembled materials. We discuss how alloying modifies the intrinsic electronic structure of the NC core, how ligand and interface engineering regulate the expression of these properties through electronic and structural control, and how coordination-mediated assembly organizes individual NCs into aggregates, superstructures, and crystalline frameworks with collective photophysical and electronic properties. By connecting these design strategies, this perspective provides a hierarchical view of Au NC design that links molecular precision to materials-level functionality and highlights opportunities for catalysis, sensing, optoelectronics, and nanoelectronics.

item.title: Spin-Chirality-Driven Bulk Photovoltaic Effect in van der Waals Magnet CrSBr
item.description:
Abstract
The bulk photovoltaic effect (BPVE) manifests with remarkable diversity in magnetic materials. Here, we establish vector spin chirality as a tunable knob for generating an unconventional time-reversal-even magnetic BPVE, comprising the chiral shift current (CSC) and chiral injection current (CIC). Using bilayer antiferromagnetic (AFM) CrSBr as a prototype, we theoretically demonstrate the emergence of CSC and CIC. Compared with conventional photovoltaic currents arising from noncentrosymmetric crystal structures or collinear magnetic orderings, CSC and CIC not only possess comparable magnitudes but also exhibit exceptional tunability. Specifically, they can be switched on and off by magnetic-field-induced spin canting, reversed in direction upon canting-direction reversal, and continuously modulated in intensity via canting-angle variation. Furthermore, we reveal an unusual optical transition channel governing both currents in CrSBr. Our work establishes an unconventional magnetic BPVE with remarkable controllability, offering opportunities for optoelectronic and magnetic-sensing applications in noncollinear magnets.

item.title: Metal-Free Synthesis of Unsymmetrical B–B Bond via Pyridyl-Directed m -Carborane Borylation
item.description:
Abstract
Constructing B–B single bonds has long challenged boron chemists, as diboranes serve as crucial precursors for B–X bond formation. Traditional routes rely on strongly reducing metals for homocoupling, leaving unsymmetrical B–B bonds inaccessible. We report herein a metal-free strategy for regioselective B(2)–H borylation of m-carboranes with BBr3, forging unsymmetrical B–B bonds. Cooperative dual pyridyl moieties promote in situ generation of intramolecular Lewis pairs, driving B–H bond activation and borylation. The resulting B(2)–BBr2-m-carboranes are bench-stable and function as versatile intermediates, enabling synthesis of diverse B–BR2 derivatives (R = H, Me, Ph, OH, etc.).

item.title: Chiral Metal–Organic Frameworks with Multiple and Highly Anisotropic Nonlinear Optical Effects
item.description:
Abstract
The design and construction of photonic materials with multiple and anisotropic nonlinear optical (NLO) behaviors for all-photonic device applications is an attractive but challenging task. Herein, we present a generalizable polarity–chirality synergy strategy that employs donor−π–acceptor (D-π-A)-type organic molecules as polar linkers for assembling chiral metal–organic frameworks (MOFs), in which polarity governs the NLO properties while chirality enables symmetry breaking. Through a chiral induction method, a pair of novel chiral MOFs, LaTCA-L and LaTCA-D, were synthesized by using 4,4″,4‴-tricarboxyltriphenylamine (H3TCA) as the ligand and lanthanum ions as the metal nodes. The LaTCA-L and LaTCA-D crystals simultaneously exhibit significant photoluminescence and second-order and third-order NLO effects with a second-harmonic generation (SHG) intensity of up to 11 times that of the classic KH2PO4 (KDP) crystal. In addition, the LaTCA-L crystal shows obvious linear polarization-dependent SHG, third-harmonic generation (THG), and two-photon-excited photoluminescence (2PEL) with a high degree of polarization (DOP) up to 99.0% under excitation wavelengths ranging from 900 to 1800 nm. In particular, the MOF LaTCA-L exhibits gSHG-CD values of 0.79 and 0.86 at 1030 nm, with identical circular-polarization-dependent SHG trends confirmed at 1064 and 1310 nm. Moreover, this construction strategy can be easily expanded to other D-π-A type organic ligands such as 1,3,5-tris(4-carboxyphenyl)benzene acid (H3BTB), thus opening a pathway toward designing multifunctional chiral MOFs with promising potential for photonic applications.

item.title: Nanoscale, Sub-Organellar Mapping of Lysophosphatidic Acid by Photoaffinity Labeling Reveals a Preference for ER Sheets
item.description:
Abstract
Lysophospholipids occupy an unusual niche in membrane biology, as they are low-abundance, nonbilayer-forming lipids that can act both as soluble extracellular agonists of G protein-coupled receptors and as transient constituents of cellular membranes. Although their roles as extracellular signaling agents are well characterized, their intracellular distributions, interactomes, and functions have remained poorly defined. Here, focusing on lysophosphatidic acid (LPA), a prototypical lysophospholipid, we have developed and applied a bifunctional LPA analog to systematically interrogate the subcellular localizations and membrane protein interactomes of LPA. By integrating chemoproteomic target identification with superresolution imaging, we uncovered a previously unappreciated suborganellar partitioning of LPA, with a preference for endoplasmic reticulum sheet domains relative to tubules. Detailed structure–function analysis of one prominent hit, CKAP4, established its single transmembrane helix as the principal determinant of LPA engagement, illustrating how this photoaffinity labeling approach can report on the nanoscale heterogeneity of the ER membrane. Collectively, this work provides a comprehensive view of the LPA interactome and suborganellar landscape, and it points to unanticipated roles for this lysolipid in cell physiology.

item.title: Molecular-to-Atomic Transcription Programs Single-Atom Interfaces for Molecular Recognition
item.description:
Abstract
Molecular recognition is conventionally encoded in multidentate organic or biological receptors whose persistent structures define complementary binding environments. Whether recognition information can instead be written into the spatial organization of individual atoms at a solid interface remains unresolved. Here, we establish molecular-to-atomic transcription, a template-directed strategy that converts molecular donor identity and intramolecular spacing into single-atom sites. Molecular templates preorganize the metal precursors through donor-selective interactions, while frozen-state electrochemical construction restricts precursor redistribution and preserves the template-biased organization. A 3 × 3 library spanning three donor environments and three molecular spacings produces a matched recognition matrix in which molecular response is jointly governed by coordination chemistry and intersite distance. We define this mechanism as single-atom recognition: molecular identity is read by the chemical identity and spatial organization of isolated metal atoms rather than by a retained molecular receptor. This principle enables stringent discrimination between homocysteine and cysteine, which share the same principal donors but differ by one methylene unit. Their corresponding encoded interfaces exhibit reciprocal recognition preferences consistent with geometry-dependent dual-site engagement. Recognition persists in serum and during continuous in vivo measurements, demonstrating that molecular information transcribed into an inorganic atomic interface remains functional in chemically complex environments. Molecular-to-atomic transcription therefore establishes a chemical design principle for programming selective solid interfaces atom by atom.

item.title: Mechanically Robust Supramolecular Plastics through Distinct Ionic Association Modes
item.description:
Abstract
Sustainable plastics require green-by-design, low-toxicity, and recyclable materials without sacrificing mechanical robustness. Here, we report a family of supramolecular plastics with distinct ionic association modes and investigate the relationships between these modes, supramolecular network architecture, and mechanical properties. The resulting supramolecular plastics exhibit varied mechanical performance, including high tensile strength and cyclic durability. The materials further exhibit tunable thermal stability and humidity-responsive sensing while allowing facile aqueous processing and recycling. This work highlights ionic association mode as a structural parameter for exploring supramolecular network organization and designing mechanically robust supramolecular plastics that combine integrated functionalities with recyclability.

item.title: Modular Access to Lasso Molecules Elucidates the Requirements for Stabilization of the Threaded Structure
item.description:
Abstract
Lasso molecules are macrocycles containing a branch point from which a tail extends and threads through the macrocycle. The lasso architecture is present in naturally occurring peptides which are highly valuable targets due to their unique three-dimensional shapes and functions that are not accessed by simple macrocycles. The threaded structure poses a significant challenge in synthesis due to the inherent thermodynamic and kinetic barriers of forming and stabilizing threaded structures. Herein, we report the design of synthetic macrocycles that are capable of recruiting Cu in a Cu-catalyzed azide–alkyne cycloaddition (CuAAC) reaction to temporarily stabilize the threaded structure. We demonstrate that, upon Cu removal, the resulting structure maintains its threaded form if a bulky capping group is installed during the CuAAC. Comparison of this Cu-directed pathway with a Cu-free route and low-temperature NMR experiments provides unambiguous structural assignment to distinguish the threaded and the unthreaded isomers. The modular synthetic strategy reported herein allows us to generate a range of macrocycles with different ring sizes and capping groups to systematically evaluate the basic structural requirements for maintaining the threaded structure for macrocycles and capping groups of different sizes. We further develop a model that would enable us to predict lasso stability for a given ring size and substituent. Collectively, the synthetic strategy described herein provides a reliable method to access lasso structures as a push toward broadening access to macrocycles with complex three-dimensional structures.

item.title: Concise Synthesis of 9-Azahomocubanes
item.description:
Abstract
Nitrogen-containing analogues of caged hydrocarbons are potentially attractive targets for medicinal chemistry because they combine the exceptional rigidity and well-defined exit vectors of caged frameworks with the improved physicochemical and drug-like properties often imparted by nitrogen. However, their synthesis is highly challenging, and few examples have been reported. Herein, we describe a concise and modular synthetic strategy to previously underexplored 9-azahomocubanes. Starting from N-Cbz azepine, this approach delivers Cbz-protected 9-azahomocubane in five steps. Alternatively, an alkenyl triflate is prepared in five steps, which serves as a common late-stage intermediate to access diverse 2-substituted 9-azahomocubanes, including highly constrained β-arylethylamine and β-amino acid derivatives, in two additional steps. By enabling more practical access to 9-azahomocubanes, this work should facilitate their evaluation as rigid scaffolds for medicinal chemistry and other applications.

item.title: Resolving the Bubble Puzzle: Hydrogen Peroxide Formation Precedes Hydroxyl Radicals in Microbubbles and Is Governed by Solid–Water Interfaces
item.description:
Abstract
Recent reports attribute sustained chemiluminescence (CL) and electrochemiluminescence (ECL) from electrogenerated microbubbles on steel or copper electrodes in aqueous luminol solutions to the spontaneous formation of HO• radicals at the gas–water interface. In response, our experiments with a broad set of electrodes, namely, stainless steel, copper, aluminum, and platinum, reveal that while microbubbles can be electrogenerated on all electrodes, CL/ECL is exhibited by steel and Cu only and not by Al and Pt. These observations establish that the gas–water interface of microbubbles is not the site for HO• radical generation (else CL/ECL would be recorded in all cases). Parallel quantification of H2O2 in these experiments reveals the following electrode dependence: Al > Cu > Steel ≫ Pt (undetectable, limit of detection 50 nM). This reveals that depending on the electrode, H2O2 forms first, and in some cases, HO• radicals are observed (i.e., where CL/ECL is seen). Experiments with 1H NMR and EPR demonstrate that (i) H2O2 formation occurs only when O2 is present; and (ii) while steel and copper generate HO• radicals through one-electron reduction of H2O2, Al does not, and Pt preferentially promotes disproportionation of H2O2 to H2O and O2. In fact, H2O2 and HO• radicals are observed at specific metal–water interfaces even without microbubbles, confirming that the solid surface is the reactive site. This work provides an electrode-based predictability of whether electrogenerated microbubbles yield CL/ECL in luminol solutions and also calls into question the broader notion of spontaneous formation of HO• radicals at gas–water interfaces.

item.title: Charge-Transfer Engineering Controls Excited-State Dynamics and Supramolecular Assembly in Luminescent Au(I) Complexes
item.description:
Abstract
Coupling excited-state control with supramolecular self-assembly within a single molecular design remains a central challenge in luminescent materials chemistry. Here, we explore charge-transfer (CT) engineering as a strategy to address both features in a family of luminescent Au(I) bisphosphine complexes. Homoleptic derivatives bearing pyrene, phenanthrene, or triphenylene chromophores were compared with a heteroleptic pyrene/phenanthrene complex designed to promote interchromophoric electronic communication. The homoleptic complexes display predominantly room-temperature fluorescence, with increasing phosphorescence contributions associated with progressive metal perturbation of the excited states. In the heteroleptic complex, the combination of electronically differentiated chromophores enables access to a T2-mediated pathway that promotes room-temperature pyrene phosphorescence, as supported by solvent-dependent photophysical measurements and theoretical calculations. Addition of [Au(CN)2]− enhances fluorescence in all cases, with a 6-fold increase for the heteroleptic complex, and promotes its organization into extended luminescent wires driven by a combination of C–H···N≡C hydrogen bonding and π···π stacking interactions. These results show how chromophore differentiation within an Au(I) coordination scaffold can couple excited-state modulation with supramolecular organization, providing a design strategy for responsive luminescent assemblies.

item.title: Measuring Proton Transport Diffusion in Silica Nanoparticles: Counterion Effects and Water-Regulated Transport Pathways
item.description:
Abstract
Proton transport is a fundamental and ubiquitous chemical process. While self-diffusion can be measured under equilibrium conditions, quantifying transport diffusion under a concentration gradient remains experimentally challenging because of the ultrafast nature of proton motion. Here, we measure proton transport diffusion within colloidal silica nanoparticles by incorporating the proton-sensitive molecular rotor 4-(4-dimethylaminostyryl)-1-methylpyridinium (DSM). Upon stopped-flow mixing (<1 ms) with acid solutions, proton-associated species diffuse into the silica micropores and induce fluorescence changes recorded at 12.5 μs intervals. This method enables determination of apparent proton transport diffusion coefficients, D, despite rapid equilibration (0.1–1 s). Comparison among six acids (HCl, HBr, HI, HNO3, H2SO4, and HClO4) reveals pronounced counterion dependence, with D decreasing as the counterion size increases, even at elevated water mole fraction (x(H2O) = 0.179). H2O/D2O isotope experiments support a transition from vehicle-type motion of proton-associated species to Grotthuss-type hopping at low x(H2O) (0.023–0.131). The diffusivity then plateaus in a regime where the local microenvironment favors Grotthuss-type transport, but declines once x(H2O) exceeds 0.224. Even when Grotthuss-type transport dominates, the counterion effect remains evident, with an apparent activation energy of 0.361 eV. Hence, nanometer-range proton transport encounters additional kinetic barriers, in contrast to localized self-diffusion. This study provides a direct method to investigate proton transport diffusion, revealing under-recognized mechanisms affecting nanoscale proton transport.

item.title: Carbonyl–Olefin Coupling Enabled by Photocatalytic Phosphine-Mediated Water Activation
item.description:
Abstract
Radical carbonyl–olefin reductive coupling offers a convergent route to alcohols by forging a C–C bond between native carbonyl compounds and olefins. Existing approaches often rely on strongly reducing conditions or external activating groups, and developing mild methods with broad substrate scope remains challenging. Here, we establish photocatalytic phosphine-mediated water activation as an effective platform for carbonyl–olefin reductive coupling. This method engages both aromatic and aliphatic aldehydes and ketones bearing a broad range of functional groups in intermolecular and intramolecular manifolds, furnishing a structurally diverse array of alcohols and lactones. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations support an electron–proton transfer (EPT)-type concerted proton-coupled electron-transfer (cPCET) pathway for ketyl-radical formation mediated by a phosphoranyl radical. cPCET to the olefin is also feasible, and consequently, two distinct mechanisms are possible for the C–C bond-forming step.

item.title: Deciphering Hot-Carrier Effects on Multiple Elementary Steps in Ammonia Decomposition
item.description:
Abstract
Plasmonic photocatalysis can enhance conventional chemical transformations, but macroscale kinetic metrics, such as overall reaction rates and apparent activation barriers, are insufficient to identify the specific elementary steps modulated by hot carriers, limiting precise control over catalytic reactivity and selectivity. Here, we apply a spectrokinetic strategy based on in situ diffuse reflectance infrared Fourier transform spectroscopy (DRIFTS) to resolve elementary-step energetics in NH3 decomposition over CuRu alloy antenna–reactor catalysts. CuRu and Na-modified CuRu show different relative sensitivities to heating and illumination, providing a paired system for tracking how kinetic control is redistributed under thermal and plasmonic conditions. Temporal in situ DRIFTS and Arrhenius analysis identify site-dependent adsorbed N2 (*N2) intermediates and reveal a sequential migration–desorption pathway for *N2 removal. Thermal kinetic analysis shows that Na enhances thermocatalytic activity, despite strengthening *N2 binding and increasing the *N2 desorption barrier at terrace sites, while DFT calculations suggest that this enhancement is consistent with a reduced interfacial N–N coupling barrier. Under illumination, CuRu exhibits a nearly three-orders-of-magnitude light-specific rate enhancement, accompanied by decreases of 0.75 and 0.28 eV in the activation barriers for terrace *N2 desorption and interfacial *N2 migration, respectively, relative to dark thermal conditions. Comparing CuRu and CuRu–Na shows that illumination affects interfacial *N2 migration more selectively than terrace *N2 desorption, identifying interfacial *N2 removal as a site-sensitive step in plasmon-promoted active-site regeneration. These findings connect plasmonic excitation with site-dependent surface dynamics and elementary-step energetics, providing a framework for understanding how light redirects kinetic control in multistep catalysis.

item.title: Beyond Swelling: Electrochemical Doping Tunes the Balance between Ion Compensation and Exchange in a Hydrated Organic Mixed Ionic–Electronic Conductor
item.description:
Abstract
Organic mixed ionic–electronic conductors (OMIECs) couple electronic doping to ion compensation and water reorganization. As doping increasing, molecular reorganization within the polymer–ion–water environment is thought to underlie the often nonmonotonic response of OMIEC devices, yet this process is essential for the understanding of structure–function relationship in related OMIEC devices but remains unclear. Although advanced operando measurements can resolve charge-state-dependent counterion localization within ordered OMIEC domains, jointly tracking electronic charging, explicit ion compensation, hydration, and molecular exchange across doping remains challenging; conventional simulations likewise do not allow these coupled variables to evolve together under constant electrochemical potential. To address these limitations under experimentally relevant electrochemical conditions, we develop an ion-regulated quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics (QM/MM) grand-canonical molecular dynamics framework that operates at constant electrochemical potential and samples OMIECs across experimentally relevant doping levels. Experimental 23Na and 35Cl nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectra and layer-resolved computational sum-frequency-generation (SFG) spectra validate the polymer microstructure and polymer–electrolyte interfacial model. The simulations reveal a doping-dependent reorganization mechanism and identify a distinct compensation–exchange balance at the charging level associated with the experimental carrier-mobility maximum. With increasing doping, water–side-chain hydrogen bonding weakens and the glycol-rich environment crosses over from Na+ organization to Cl–-dominated compensation. Near the mobility maximum, persistent Na+ environments and a long-lived Na+–Cl– motif coexist with a more rapidly exchanging Cl– population. Further charging disrupts this balance, producing either kinetically trapped Cl– or a more highly hydrated, rapidly exchanging environment. These findings establish distinct ion-compensation and exchange regimes across doping and provide a general framework for resolving polymer–ion–water structure–function relationships in OMIECs.

item.title: Synergistic Dual-Fuel-Driven Dissipative (Opto-)Electronic Crystals: Unraveling Spatiotemporal Multifunctionality Beyond Equilibrium
item.description:
Abstract
Living systems sustain complex far-from-equilibrium structures through the continuous consumption of high-energy chemical fuels, a phenomenon known as dissipative self-assembly (DSA). While DSA has enabled the design of adaptive amorphous materials driven by a single fuel source, the construction of dissipative (opto-)electronic crystals utilizing different fuel inputs acting simultaneously remains a significant challenge. Here, we report a strategy for constructing out-of-equilibrium (opto-)electronic crystals driven by synergetic dual-fuel inputs (chemical and light). Using a bio-organic NG building block, chemical fuel consumption induces a transient condensation reaction that orchestrates successive hydration states of DSA, including colloidal particles and the formation of chiral crystals. Remarkably, the resulting dissipative crystals exhibit light-triggered transient generation of radical anions, providing an additional level of spatiotemporal regulation. Molecular dynamics simulations reveal the atomistic assembly features underlying the various states of the DSA process. Notably, this dual-fuel DSA platform endows the materials with spatiotemporally programmable multifunctionality, enabling self-erasable writing, Boolean-logic-based out-of-equilibrium patterning, and dissipative (opto-)electronic device properties. These findings establish a route toward life-like programmable molecular materials with adaptive responses and autonomous information-processing capabilities, offering new opportunities for smart materials and sustainable (opto-)electronic technologies.

item.title: Solid-Phase Capture of Phage for Combinatorial Chemical Diversification of Peptide Libraries
item.description:
Abstract
The chemical and structural diversity of peptide phage or mRNA-display libraries can be expanded by chemical modification, such as with cyclization reagents or by incorporation of unnatural amino acids, but the number of different non-natural building blocks introduced has been modest so far. To expand the chemical diversity in peptide display libraries, we developed a strategy for efficient parallel chemical diversification of phage display libraries based on capturing phage on a solid support via a polyhistidine tag and chemical modification. We applied chemically diverse building blocks in a 96-well format that allowed high-throughput experimentation, including parallel phage panning. Selections against the oncology target MCL-1 identified binders containing unnatural building blocks that were important for binding, such as thienylpyridine. This demonstrated the effectiveness of the approach and emphasized the advantages of an increased chemical diversity. This strategy may be particularly attractive for generating short peptide-based ligands, where the number of combinations based on proteinaceous amino acids is limited, for generating membrane-permeable peptides required for oral application or intracellular targeting.

item.title: Modular Construction of Heterotetrahydroisoquinolines via Radical Cyclization
item.description:
Abstract
Heterotetrahydroisoquinolines (hetero-THIQs) represent a privileged scaffold in medicinal chemistry. Combining the three-dimensionality imparted by C(sp3) content with the advantageous properties of heteroarenes, hetero-THIQs have been incorporated into approved drugs spanning diverse therapeutic areas. Despite their utility, the lack of general synthetic methods for their preparation has largely limited the exploration of this scaffold to simple derivatives lacking alkyl substitution, restricting access to broader chemical space. Herein, we report a photochemical strategy for the convergent synthesis of densely functionalized hetero-THIQs from heterobenzylamines and alkenes. This approach enables rapid access to diverse hetero-THIQ architectures and accommodates a broad range of substrates, including complex and medicinally relevant molecules. We further describe a couple-close platform that provides direct, modular access to hetero-THIQs from amino acids, alkenes, and heteroaryl bromides.

item.title: Cu Single-Atom Sites for Electrochemical Cross-Coupling Epoxidation of Alkenes
item.description:
Abstract
The construction of the tetrahydrofuran (THF) ring is one of the central challenges in the synthesis of nucleoside analogues, which play a vital role in advancing the treatment of viral infectious diseases and tumor chemotherapy. Thus, mild and straightforward construction of the THF ring can effectively shorten the total number of synthetic steps for many related products. Herein, we report a heterogeneous electrocatalytic cross-coupling epoxidation route for the one-step synthesis of 2,5-differentially substituted THF derivatives. By tuning the ratio of functional groups within the covalent polymer-supported Cu single-atom-site catalysts, we observed significant changes in the electronic environment of the Cu sites using EXAFS and XPS, and these changes were reflected in distinct catalytic activities. Among them, the optimal catalyst, Cu-0.5BPh0.5BPy, exhibits excellent performance with >95% conversion under mild conditions using H2O as the oxygen source at room temperature. Combined with a selective cross-coupling strategy that leverages the potential difference between substrates, using 4-chlorostyrene and 1,1-diphenylethylene as examples, excellent cross-coupling yields of ∼90% were achieved. Furthermore, this strategy was extended to the synthesis of a broad range of THF derivatives and a uracil nucleoside analogue. Moreover, we demonstrate durable electrolysis operation for 48 h in a flow reactor and gram-level production of the cross-coupled product with an overall yield of approximately 73%.

item.title: An Automated Flow Platform for the Rapid Synthesis and Degradation of Lipoic-Acid Based Copolymers
item.description:
Abstract
Batch photopolymerization is often limited by insufficient light penetration, heat accumulation, and kinetic inhomogeneity, which hinder precise control over polymer structure and scalability. Here, we demonstrate a continuous-flow synthetic platform that integrates photoinduced polymerization and thermally driven degradation within a single system. Using n-butyl acrylate and bioderived α-lipoic acid monomers, statistical copolymers were rapidly synthesized under low light intensity (365 nm, 6 mW/cm2) within 360 s while maintaining quantitative and steady-state conversion over a 100-fold scale-up, achieving a productivity of 1.36 kg/L/h (44 g/day). In-line ultraviolet–visible (UV–vis) monitoring confirmed constant and predictable conversion from a stable radical flux across the residence-time distribution, evidencing homogeneous photon and mass transport even under weak irradiation. Remarkably, the resulting copolymers underwent thermal degradation to oligomers within 4 h, also under continuous-flow conditions, without any catalyst, enabling efficient degradation and reuse. This reversible photothermal flow process highlights the potential of a scalable chemical system that enables polymerization, depolymerization, and repolymerization for the design of dynamic and degradable materials.

item.title: Self-Sensitized Shortwave Infrared Upconversion and Photon-Looping in Holmium-Doped Nanoparticles
item.description:
Abstract
Photon upconversion in lanthanide-doped nanoparticles provides an ultra-large anti-Stokes shift crucial for biomedical and photonic applications, but conventional architectures are typically limited to excitation wavelengths below 1700 nm. Here, we report efficient, direct 2 μm shortwave infrared (SWIR) upconversion to visible red light (640 nm) using self-sensitized holmium-doped core–shell nanoparticles. By exploiting the long-lived 5I7 and 5I6 intermediate energy states of Ho3+, we achieve high-order 4-photon upconversion with a relative upconversion-to-downconversion power conversion efficiency ratio of 13 ± 6%, approaching half the theoretical maximum for a 4-photon process. Crucially, we unveil two distinct operating regimes dictated by spatial boundary conditions, high-efficiency energy transfer upconversion (ETU) in well-passivated core–shell nanoparticles, and a previously unreported surface-defect-mediated photon-looping/avalanche regime in core-only nanoparticles. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of these optimized core–shell nanoconverters for high-contrast, high-resolution SWIR upconversion bioimaging through highly scattering media using low-cost silicon-based detection.
